# A Map for the Way Home

The first map arrived on a Thursday, folded into quarters and pushed under the door of the repair shop.

It showed the town as it had been thirty years ago. There was the old cinema, now a pharmacy; the orchard, now a row of houses; and the footbridge over the canal, removed after a flood. Whoever had drawn it had used blue ink for the streets and green pencil for the gardens. A thin red line began at the train station, wandered past the cinema, and stopped at a house on Bell Street.

On the back, in small handwriting, were the words: *I knew the way once.*

Nell spent the morning wondering whether someone expected her to repair it.

People brought her maps for all sorts of reasons. She had learned to flatten a water-damaged atlas without tearing its pages, to reinforce a crease with paper fine enough to disappear, and to remove old tape that had hardened into yellow strips. Most of her work came from museums, surveyors, and people who had inherited drawers they were finally ready to sort. She liked that maps could be useful long after their information became wrong. A vanished road might explain why a wall curved strangely. An old field name might outlast every tree in it.

But the map under the door had no sender, and she could find nothing broken about it except the journey.

At lunch, she walked to Bell Street. The house at the end of the red line was a hairdresser’s now. Its front window was crowded with photographs of elaborate wedding hair, and a woman inside was sweeping dark clippings into a neat pile. Nell crossed the road before the woman could ask if she needed an appointment.

The following Thursday, another map appeared.

This one was recent, printed from a phone and covered in annotations. Its owner had crossed out the shortest route between a block of flats and the public swimming pool. In the margin, someone had written, *Too many stairs*, and drawn a slower route through the park. Near a bench by the duck pond, a question mark had been pressed hard enough to leave an impression on the other side.

Nell recognized the handwriting. Mrs. Vale, who lived above the bakery, wrote notes with that same decisive slant. She had come into the shop the previous winter to ask whether Nell could repair a recipe book whose cover had pulled free. Her husband had died in November. By spring, she had begun swimming on Wednesday mornings, or said she meant to.

Nell climbed the stairs above the bakery that evening with the map in her bag. Mrs. Vale opened the door wearing a dressing gown and one shoe.

“I was going out,” she said, looking at the shoe.

“I think you dropped this.”

Mrs. Vale studied the map. “No. I threw that away.”

“It was under my door.”

For a moment Mrs. Vale looked alarmed. Then she said, “Well, it knows more than I do.”

Nell turned the paper over. “Were you trying to find a route to the pool?”

“I know where the pool is. I’ve lived here forty-two years.” Mrs. Vale held the door open wider. “It’s the first time I’ve gone that’s difficult. If I get tired halfway, I have to get back. I thought I’d sit by the pond, but the bench may be gone. They’re always moving things.”

Nell had passed the pond that morning. “It’s still there.”

Mrs. Vale nodded, relieved in a way she seemed to find embarrassing. “Good.”

On Wednesday, Nell saw her from across the park. She was sitting on the bench in a coat and swimming shoes, eating a pear. Nell didn’t interrupt her. When she passed again an hour later, Mrs. Vale was gone, and a line of wet footprints led from the pool entrance across the pavement.

After that, maps kept arriving.

Some had lost nothing more than a name. A visitor had marked the place where he had eaten an excellent sandwich but forgotten the café’s street. A little girl had drawn every corner between her house and her friend’s, then left a large blank where a row of garages had been demolished. Nell recognized the demolished garages and wrote *building site* lightly in pencil. She waited outside the shop the next afternoon, hoping the girl would come past. She did, carrying a violin case nearly as long as her arm. Nell gave the map back and watched her check the new route with one finger.

Others were harder. One map showed the road to a village that no longer existed; a reservoir covered it now. Another was a hand-drawn plan of a hospital, annotated with arrows that led reliably to a room whose doors had since been renumbered. Nell called the hospital and asked about the room. It had been a family waiting area, the receptionist told her. The chairs were now on another floor.

Nell kept the maps in a shallow drawer beside her workbench. She meant to find out who was delivering them. Each Thursday she tried arriving earlier, but the paper was always waiting when she unlocked the shop. Once she stayed all night, dozing in her chair while the streetlights turned the windows orange. At dawn she opened the door to buy a coffee. When she returned, a map lay on the floor. She looked up and down the empty street, annoyed at herself for laughing.

Across the road was a bus stop. For years, Nell’s father had waited there every morning with his lunch in a square metal tin. He had been a cartographer for the county until the county decided it no longer needed so many. Then he worked at a garden centre, where customers asked him about compost and occasionally recognized his name from the maps they kept in their cars.

He had taught Nell how to use a compass on long walks when she was a child. First they would find north. Then he would turn the map until its printed roads matched the roads under their feet.

“Now,” he would say, “where are we?”

She always wanted to point to the place they were going. He would make her find the place they stood.

After he died, Nell opened the repair shop in the small unit opposite the bus stop. People assumed she had followed him into maps. She had, though not quite in the way they meant. She liked working at a table where she could take her time, with a window that let her see the bus arrive. If she was cleaning a map of the county, she sometimes found one of his careful labels.

One Thursday in June, the map under the door was blank.

It was a square of thick cream paper, marked only with a blue dot near the centre. Nell held it up to the window, looking for pencil lines or printing that had faded. There were none. On the reverse, someone had written: *Where should we put the bench?*

She knew at once which bench.

The council had removed it from the square in April. Its slats had rotted, and orange fencing had gone up around it for a week before a truck came to take it away. Since then people had stood by the flower bed to eat their lunches. Mr. Hadi, who sold fruit at the market, sometimes brought a folding chair for his mother. The square looked almost the same without the bench, but people passed through it faster.

Nell carried the paper outside and stood at the blue dot. It placed her beside the bus stop, where there was already a seat: a narrow metal one under a shelter. She walked to the square and imagined the paper laid over the ground. It wasn’t drawn to scale, but the question stayed with her. The old bench had caught the afternoon sun. Perhaps it had also blocked the way when market stalls were being set up. She had never asked.

Mr. Hadi was stacking peaches in shallow crates. When Nell asked him where he would put a new bench, he looked around thoughtfully.

“Near my stall,” he said. “For my mother. But she would say under the tree.”

“Which tree?”

“That’s the problem.” He pointed toward the churchyard, beyond the square. “There’s shade there in the morning. None here when it gets hot.”

Nell asked the woman opening the bookshop. She wanted the bench opposite her window, where she could see whether anyone had left a bag behind. A delivery driver wanted it away from the loading bay. Two schoolchildren wanted it beside the fountain, which had not run for years. Mrs. Vale wanted it halfway between the bakery and the pool.

By the end of the day, Nell’s blank paper was crowded with arrows. She copied it onto a larger sheet and taped the sheet to her shop window, where anyone could add a mark. Someone drew a dog. Someone wrote, *Could we have two?*

At the next council meeting, Nell sat between Mr. Hadi and a man who had come to complain about a drain. She expected to be told there was no money. Instead, the councilor responsible for the square showed her a plan: a new bench had been ordered, but work crews couldn’t install it until August. They had chosen the old spot because that was where the paving had been reinforced.

“Could it go somewhere else?” Nell asked.

“Possibly. We’d need to check access. Why?”

Nell unfolded her crowded paper. The councilor leaned forward. Mr. Hadi pointed out where his mother liked to sit. The man with the drain problem, who walked through the square daily, said a bench by the fountain would leave room for the market. By the end of the discussion, the councilor had agreed to meet them there on Saturday.

That Thursday, no map came. Nell was disappointed, though she had enough work to fill the week. She spent Friday evening repairing a harbor chart. Its previous owner had used it at sea; salt had made the paper stiff, and one edge was worn soft from being folded and unfolded with damp hands. She worked until she could safely close it again.

Saturday was bright and windless. The councilor arrived with a tape measure. Mrs. Vale brought a flask of tea. Mr. Hadi’s mother tested each proposed site by sitting on the folding chair while everyone else stood back. She chose a place near the fountain, turned slightly toward the market.

“You can see who’s coming,” she said.

The councilor measured the distance to the footpath and said it might work. He would have the crew check. Mrs. Vale poured the last tea into a paper cup for him, and they all went home.

The bench arrived in August. It was plain wood, sturdy enough to bear the bags of anyone who had overestimated their strength at the market. On its first afternoon, Mr. Hadi’s mother sat beside a teenage boy eating chips. Neither of them seemed to know the other. When the boy got up, she moved her shopping into the space he had left and called across the square to tell her son she would be another ten minutes.

Nell saw them from her shop window. Under her workbench, the shallow drawer was nearly full.

She had tried to return every map she could, but some had no name attached. People began to ask about them after seeing the bench drawing in her window. Nell made a notice explaining that she had found several maps and would gladly give them back to their owners. A few were claimed. The rest remained in the drawer, held flat beneath sheets of clean paper.

In September, one of them brought a stranger to her door.

He was a tall man with a bicycle helmet in his hand. He pointed to the old map of Bell Street, which Nell had hung in the window because she hoped someone would recognize the handwriting.

“My mother drew that,” he said.

Nell invited him in. His mother had grown up in the house that was now a hairdresser’s. She had moved away after marrying and had returned to town that summer for a visit. Her son said she had tried to walk from the station to Bell Street without looking at a modern map. She was certain she remembered the way. At the old cinema, she became confused, went back to the station, and took a taxi.

“She drew this when she got home,” he said. “Then she decided it was silly and put it in the recycling.”

“Does she know it’s here?”

“She saw it yesterday.” He smiled. “She was very cross with me for telling you.”

Nell took the map down. “Would she like it back?”

“She asked if you could fix the route.”

“The streets are different.”

“She knows. She wants to try again.”

Nell cleared a space on her workbench. With the man beside her, she laid a sheet of thin tracing paper over his mother’s map. He remembered the street where the cinema had stood, and Nell knew which path cut through the new housing where the orchard had been. Together they drew a route that stayed as close as it could to the red line. At the canal they marked the nearest bridge, a little farther west. Nell wrote the new street names on the tracing paper so the old ones would still show beneath.

When the man came to collect it two days later, he brought a photograph of his mother outside the hairdresser’s. The woman who had been sweeping was in the picture too. She had let her visitor look into the back room, where a piece of the old kitchen tile was still visible beneath a cabinet.

That night, Nell took all the unclaimed maps from the drawer and spread them across the shop floor. From above, the papers looked like pieces of several different towns. There were familiar roads and invented shortcuts, remembered doors, uncertain benches, and blank places where someone had not yet looked. She sat among them for a long time, trying to decide what work they needed from her.

In the morning, she put them away. She could not always know who had drawn them, and it would be wrong to fill in a stranger’s blanks merely because she could. She left a pencil and a stack of fresh paper on the table by the door, with a small card that said: *If you need help finding a place, come in.*

People did. A delivery rider asked her to mark an entrance hidden behind an office block. A woman and her brother came in with their grandfather’s sketch of a lane from his childhood. Nell could not find it in the current street plan, but she found its name on an old survey sheet her father had kept. Mrs. Vale stopped by on her way to the pool and drew a firm line through the park for someone who was new to town.

Nell still checked the floor each Thursday when she opened the shop. Sometimes there was a map, sometimes only a leaf blown in when she lifted the door. She never discovered who had brought the first one. Whoever it was had found the right place to leave it: a shop with enough table space to open a map, and someone willing to look closely before drawing a new line.
